Let me tell you how I plan a congress day, because my first congress was a disaster. I tried to attend everything, and at six o'clock in the evening I remembered nothing. Now I do the opposite. The night before, I read the program and I decide on three sessions. Three, not ten. I avoid choosing two talks in the same hour, because then I spend the hour walking between rooms. And I always keep one hour free in the afternoon, for the corridor. The corridor is where the real work happens. People ask me if I miss good talks. Of course I do. But I manage to have three real conversations, and in December I still remember all of them.

I have two recommendations for anybody standing at a poster for the first time. First, do not read your own poster to people. They can read. Instead, ask them one question: what brings you to this topic? Then you know what to say and what to leave out. Second, I recommend preparing three versions of your work: thirty seconds, two minutes, and ten minutes. You decide which one to use after the first question, never before it. And there is one thing I avoid completely: apologizing for my English. Nobody in that room is thinking about your grammar. They are thinking about your data. Keep talking, and they will stay.
